name: German
intro: Start with standard German. Keep noun gender and plural with every entry, learn verbs with their complements and use authentic writing to develop register. Austrian and Swiss standard German share the main grammatical system but differ in vocabulary and conventions; Swiss German dialect comprehension requires separate listening. Swiss standard spelling generally uses ss rather than ß. The lessons below move from sentence control to formal analysis.

foundation.name: German
notes: The core alphabet has 26 letters. Ä, Ö and Ü are umlaut letters; ß is an additional character. Letter names are for spelling aloud. In words, J usually sounds like English y, W like English v, V often like f, and Z like /ts/. Learn each noun with its article and plural: das Buch, die Bücher.

Long and short vowels can distinguish words. ie usually represents long /iː/; ei sounds like English eye; eu and äu like the vowel in boy. sch is /ʃ/. After a, o, u, ch is the back sound /x/; after front vowels it is often /ç/. Round the lips while saying e for ö and i for ü; an English spelling approximation cannot replace hearing them.

Nouns start with a capital letter. Double consonants often signal a preceding short vowel. ß generally follows a long vowel or diphthong; ss generally follows a short vowel. In Switzerland, ss replaces ß. Stress is often early, but borrowed words and prefixes can change it.
building: Haus + Tür → Haustür = front door. The last noun is the head and determines gender: die Tür → die Haustür. Some compounds need linking material: Arbeit + s + Zimmer → Arbeitszimmer.
freundlich = friendly; unfreundlich = unfriendly; Freundlichkeit = friendliness. Record the suffix with its meaning and word class: -keit usually makes a feminine noun.
Ich lerne Deutsch. = I am learning German. Heute lerne ich Deutsch. = Today I am learning German. A first-position time expression does not move the finite verb out of second position.

sections.title: Sounds, spelling and noun inventory
sections.explanation:
German vowel length can distinguish words, and umlauts are separate vowel qualities rather than decorative marks. Learn /y/ for ü and /ø/ or /œ/ for ö by rounding the lips while keeping a front-vowel tongue position. The ich-Laut /ç/ and ach-Laut /x/ occur in different environments, with regional variation. Final obstruent devoicing means written d, b and g can be pronounced like their voiceless partners at the end of a syllable.
Nouns are capitalised. Learn der Tisch, die Tische; die Frage, die Fragen; das Buch, die Bücher. Gender is partly predictable from suffixes, such as feminine -ung and neuter -chen, but semantic gender and grammatical gender are not identical. Plural patterns require lexical learning. Do not infer a noun's gender from its English translation.
examples: die Entscheidung, die Entscheidungen
decision, decisions
-ung is a productive feminine noun ending.
das Mädchen, die Mädchen
girl, girls
-chen makes the grammatical gender neuter; the plural is unchanged.
exercises: What information belongs on a German noun card?
Article, singular, plural, meaning and one useful collocation. Include relevant pronunciation if spelling is misleading.
Why is das Mädchen grammatically possible?
The diminutive suffix -chen determines neuter gender, independently of the person's natural gender.

sections.title: Cases and determiners
sections.explanation:
German cases show grammatical relationships. Nominative normally marks the subject; accusative many direct objects; dative many indirect objects and prepositional complements; genitive possession or other formal relationships. Verb and preposition government must be learned: helfen takes dative; sehen normally takes accusative. Masculine singular articles show der, den, dem, des. Feminine: die, die, der, der. Neuter: das, das, dem, des. Plural: die, die, den, der; dative plural often adds -n to the noun where possible.
With two-way prepositions such as in, an and auf, accusative marks a directed change into a spatial relation, dative a location within it. Movement alone is not the deciding test: Ich laufe im Park describes running inside the park with dative. Other prepositions have fixed case: mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu with dative; durch, für, gegen, ohne, um with accusative.
examples: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.
I put the book onto the table.
Accusative marks the directed placement.
Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
The book lies on the table.
Dative marks the location.
exercises: Choose: Ich helfe der / die Kollegin.
Der Kollegin. Helfen governs dative, and feminine dative singular is der.
Why is Ich laufe im Park dative although running is movement?
The action occurs within an existing location. The sentence does not express a change into that spatial relation.

sections.title: Adjective endings and noun phrases
sections.explanation:
Adjective endings distribute grammatical information across the noun phrase. After a definite article, the article usually carries the strongest case/gender marking, leaving the adjective with -e or -en. After ein, the adjective must sometimes supply a missing ending: ein guter Plan, ein gutes Buch. Without an article, the adjective normally carries a strong ending: mit gutem Grund.
Read phrases as systems rather than memorising an isolated ending. Der gute Plan is nominative masculine; den guten Plan is accusative masculine; mit einem guten Plan is dative. Nominalised adjectives retain adjectival inflection: etwas Neues, die Verantwortlichen. Long formal noun phrases can contain multiple modifiers, so identify the head noun before interpreting the whole phrase.
examples: mit einem klaren Ziel
with a clear goal
Mit requires dative; einem marks neuter dative; klaren uses -en.
ein überzeugendes Ergebnis
a convincing result
The adjective supplies neuter nominative/accusative -es after ein.
exercises: Complete: wegen des neu__ Gesetzes.
Wegen des neuen Gesetzes. After des, the adjective takes -en; Gesetz has genitive -es.
Explain etwas Wichtiges.
Wichtig is nominalised after etwas and receives the appropriate strong ending; the noun-like adjective is capitalised.

sections.title: Verb position and clause architecture
sections.explanation:
In a declarative main clause, the finite verb occupies the second constituent position, not necessarily the second word. Heute beginnt die Sitzung; Die Sitzung beginnt heute. A fronted multiword phrase still counts as one constituent. Yes/no questions commonly place the finite verb first. In many subordinate clauses introduced by weil, dass or obwohl, the finite verb appears at the end.
The sentence bracket separates the finite verb from an infinitive, participle or separable prefix: Wir haben den Bericht geprüft; Wir rufen morgen an. Formal verb clusters with modals and perfect tense require additional study, including the replacement infinitive. Do not apply an English subject-verb-object template inside every German clause. Identify the finite verb and clause boundary before translating.
examples: Obwohl die Daten unvollständig sind, beginnt die Prüfung.
Although the data are incomplete, the review begins.
The subordinate clause occupies the first main-clause constituent; beginnt remains second.
Wir müssen den Bericht sorgfältig prüfen.
We must examine the report carefully.
Finite modal in second position; lexical infinitive closes the bracket.
exercises: Reorder: Morgen / wir / beginnen / mit der Arbeit.
Morgen beginnen wir mit der Arbeit. Fronted morgen is followed by the finite verb.
Combine using weil: Ich bleibe. Ich brauche weitere Informationen.
Ich bleibe, weil ich weitere Informationen brauche. Brauche closes the subordinate clause.

sections.title: Tense, passive and reported speech
sections.explanation:
German conversational narration often uses Perfekt, while written narration often favours Präteritum; sein, haben and modal verbs commonly use Präteritum in speech too. These are tendencies, not rigid genre bans. Future meaning frequently uses present tense with a time expression. Futur I can also express an inference.
The event passive uses werden + past participle: Der Bericht wird geprüft. The state passive uses sein: Der Bericht ist geprüft. In the perfect event passive, worden differs from the ordinary geworden. Konjunktiv I can mark reported speech without committing the writer to its truth: Sie erklärt, die Daten seien vollständig. Where forms are ambiguous, Konjunktiv II or other reporting strategies can help; the register and context matter.
examples: Die Daten werden geprüft / Die Daten sind geprüft.
The data are being checked / The data have the status of being checked.
Process passive contrasts with a resulting state.
Der Autor schreibt, das Ergebnis sei vorläufig.
The author writes that the result is provisional.
Sei is Konjunktiv I of sein and marks reported speech.
exercises: Make a passive: Das Team prüft den Bericht.
Der Bericht wird vom Team geprüft. The former object becomes the subject.
Report without endorsing: Sie sagt: Ich habe keine Fehler gefunden.
Sie sagt, sie habe keine Fehler gefunden. Habe marks indirect report; it does not independently verify the claim.

sections.title: Conditionals, modality and polite disagreement
sections.explanation:
Konjunktiv II expresses irreality, hypothetical reasoning and politeness. Wäre, hätte and könnte are central forms. Würde + infinitive is common but should not displace every established simple form. Past counterfactuals combine hätte or wäre with the participle: Wenn ich das gewusst hätte, wäre ich geblieben.
Modal particles such as doch, ja, eben and wohl shape interpersonal meaning and inference. Their translation depends on context; do not assign one English equivalent to each. Das ist ja interessant may signal a reaction to newly encountered information, not simply yes. For professional disagreement, give the point of agreement and the precise reservation before proposing a change.
examples: Könnten Sie erläutern, wie dieser Wert berechnet wurde?
Could you explain how this value was calculated?
Konjunktiv II softens the request; the embedded clause is verb-final.
Wenn die Stichprobe größer gewesen wäre, hätten wir präzisere Schätzungen erhalten.
If the sample had been larger, we would have obtained more precise estimates.
Past counterfactual; the conclusion remains hypothetical.
exercises: Write a polite request with könnte.
Könnten Sie mir bitte die Unterlagen schicken? A conventional concise request; other phrasings are valid.
What does wohl do in Das wird wohl stimmen?
It commonly marks a tentative inference: that is probably correct. Context can change the nuance.

sections.title: Relative clauses and compressed academic prose
sections.explanation:
A relative pronoun agrees in gender and number with its antecedent, but its case comes from its role inside the relative clause. Der Bericht, den ich gelesen habe uses accusative den because the pronoun is the object of gelesen. Die Person, mit der ich gesprochen habe uses dative after mit. Do not choose case from the antecedent's role in the main clause.
Formal German often compresses information into participial noun modifiers: die unter bestimmten Bedingungen erhobenen Daten. Expand the phrase into a relative clause to check understanding. Nominalisation can make prose compact but conceal agents or temporal relationships. Identify compounds from the rightmost head: Forschungsfrage is a kind of Frage, not a kind of Forschung.
examples: die unter kontrollierten Bedingungen erhobenen Daten
the data collected under controlled conditions
The participial modifier precedes the noun; erhoben is the past participle of erheben.
Die Methode, deren Grenzen bekannt sind, wurde angepasst.
The method whose limitations are known was adapted.
Deren marks the genitive relationship inside the relative clause.
exercises: Expand die gestern veröffentlichten Ergebnisse.
Die Ergebnisse, die gestern veröffentlicht wurden. A relative clause makes the passive event explicit.
Choose: Der Kollege, dem / den ich vertraue.
Dem. Vertrauen governs dative inside the relative clause.

sections.title: Argument, register and advanced reading
sections.explanation:
Distinguish daher for consequence, dennoch for concession, hingegen for contrast and insofern for a limited respect or conditional relationship. Technical nouns need conventional collocations: eine Hypothese aufstellen, eine Entscheidung treffen, eine Untersuchung durchführen. Neutral standard writing differs from colloquial regional speech; both deserve exposure.
Original teaching passage: Eine Erklärung kann plausibel sein, ohne dass sie durch die verfügbaren Daten eindeutig bestätigt wird. Entscheidend ist daher nicht nur, ob eine Hypothese zu den Beobachtungen passt, sondern auch, welche alternativen Erklärungen ausgeschlossen werden können. Je genauer die Voraussetzungen beschrieben werden, desto leichter lässt sich beurteilen, wie weit die Ergebnisse verallgemeinert werden dürfen.
The passage separates plausibility from evidential confirmation, then limits generalisation. Je ... desto expresses a proportional comparison. Dürfen here concerns what inference is warranted, not an ordinary permission request.
examples: Je genauer die Voraussetzungen beschrieben werden, desto leichter lässt sich die Aussage beurteilen.
The more precisely the assumptions are described, the easier the claim is to assess.
Paired comparative structure plus lässt sich + infinitive for assessability.
Die Befunde deuten auf einen Zusammenhang hin.
The findings suggest an association.
Hindeuten auf is weaker than proving a causal relation.
exercises: Translate the main caution in the passage.
A plausible explanation is not necessarily unambiguously confirmed by the available evidence. Alternative explanations and scope must be assessed.
Write a 120-word critique using dennoch and hingegen.
Check connector logic, verb-second main clauses, accurate cases and a distinction between evidence and interpretation. Use the revision rubric in the study guide.

rules.title: Articles in context
rules.explanation: A German article marks gender, number and case together. Die can be feminine singular or plural; der can occur in several case/gender combinations. Identify the noun and its sentence role before choosing an ending.

examples.native: Zwingen Sie mich nicht, das zu essen!
examples.translation: Don't make me eat this.

examples.native: Der Vater geht im Park spazieren.
examples.translation: My father is taking a walk in the park.

examples.native: Er war der einzige Betrunkene auf der Feier.
examples.translation: He was the only one drunk at the party.

rules.title: Indefinite articles
rules.explanation: Ein introduces an indefinite singular noun. Its endings depend on gender and case; some forms have no overt ending. There is no ordinary plural ein article. Learn a noun together with gender and plural.

examples.native: Japaner und Briten warten an Bushaltestellen normalerweise in einer Schlange.
examples.translation: Japanese and British people usually wait at a bus stop in a queue.

examples.native: Ich bin es gewohnt, einen Lastwagen zu fahren.
examples.translation: I am used to driving a truck.

examples.native: Tom trägt eine Sonnenbrille.
examples.translation: Tom is wearing sunglasses.

rules.title: Personal pronoun forms
rules.explanation: Pronouns change form with their grammatical role. Ich is nominative, mich accusative, mir dative. Sie can mean she, they or polite you; spelling and context distinguish the uses.

examples.native: Hast du Vorsätze fürs neue Jahr?
examples.translation: Have you made any New Year's resolutions?

examples.native: Tom gab seinen Freunden gegenüber damit an, mit wie vielen Mädchen er schon geschlafen habe.
examples.translation: Tom bragged to his friends about all the girls he had slept with.

examples.native: Ich werde Tom nicht erlauben zu gehen.
examples.translation: I won't allow Tom to go.

rules.title: Adjectives in noun phrases
rules.explanation: Attributive adjectives take endings after the determiner. Compare ein gutes Buch, das gute Buch and mit einem guten Buch. Predicative adjectives normally stay uninflected: Das Buch ist gut.

examples.native: Tom verglich ein drei Jahre altes Foto von Mary mit einem aktuellen.
examples.translation: Tom compared a picture taken of Mary three years ago with one that had been taken recently.

examples.native: Zuerst fiel mir das große Sofa auf. Der Lederbezug war in einem schlichten Farbton gehalten, die Sitzfläche und Rückenlehne sahen bequem aus.
examples.translation: The first thing that came to my attention was the large sofa. It was covered in sober coloured leather, the seat and the back both looked wide and comfortable.

examples.native: Diese gute Zeit wird nicht lange währen.
examples.translation: These good times won't last long.

rules.title: Present forms of sein
rules.explanation: Sein is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir/sie sind, ihr seid. A finite verb agrees with the subject. In a main statement it normally occupies the second constituent position.

examples.native: Warum sind einige Übersetzungen ausgegraut?
examples.translation: Why are some translations in grey?

examples.native: Tom ist faul.
examples.translation: Tom is lazy.

examples.native: Tom ist ziemlich sarkastisch.
examples.translation: Tom is quite sarcastic.

rules.title: Present forms of haben
rules.explanation: Haben can express possession or serve as a perfect auxiliary. Identify whether a participle is also present. The finite form agrees with the subject even when an infinitive or participle stands later.

examples.native: Wie viele Bundesstaaten hat Indien?
examples.translation: How many states does India have?

examples.native: Ich habe nicht viel Geld auf meinem Konto.
examples.translation: I don't have much money in my bank account.

examples.native: Erst gestern hat er sie wahrgenommen.
examples.translation: It was not until yesterday that he noticed her.

rules.title: Modal verbs
rules.explanation: Modals express ability, necessity, permission, reported obligation or intention. A following ordinary infinitive normally has no zu and goes late in the clause. Nicht müssen means lack of necessity; nicht dürfen means prohibition.

examples.native: Tom will sich entschuldigen.
examples.translation: Tom is going to apologize.

examples.native: In diesem Buch steht, dass Elefanten über hundert Jahre alt werden können.
examples.translation: This book says that elephants live to be over 100 years old.

examples.native: Tom kann nur mit Mühe mit dem Rest der Klasse Schritt halten.
examples.translation: Tom has trouble keeping up with the rest of the class.

rules.title: Negation with nicht and kein
rules.explanation: Kein negates many indefinite noun phrases; nicht negates a predicate or another constituent. Placement controls scope. Compare Ich kaufe kein Buch with Ich kaufe das Buch nicht.

examples.native: Tom konnte sich nicht vorstellen, jemanden zu erschießen.
examples.translation: Tom couldn't imagine himself shooting anyone.

examples.native: Tom konnte nicht alle Fragen Marias beantworten.
examples.translation: Tom couldn't answer all of Mary's questions.

examples.native: Dafür bezahle ich nicht!
examples.translation: I won't pay for that.

rules.title: Subordinate clause connectors
rules.explanation: A subordinating connector introduces a clause whose finite verb normally comes at the end. Ob introduces an indirect yes/no question. Wenn and als differ in temporal uses; als normally locates a single past occasion.

examples.native: Du wusstest, dass da passieren wird, stimmt's?
examples.translation: You knew this was going to happen, right?

examples.native: Tom kam gerade, als ich ging.
examples.translation: Tom came just as I was leaving.

examples.native: Die Nachricht erwies sich als falsch.
examples.translation: The news turned out false.

rules.title: Coordinating connectors
rules.explanation: Coordinating connectors do not impose subordinate verb-final order. Sondern corrects a preceding negated alternative. Denn gives a reason with main-clause order.

examples.native: Tom und Maria liefen ins Wasser.
examples.translation: Tom and Mary ran into the water.

examples.native: Das Mädchen wurde abgelenkt und verlor ihre Eltern aus den Augen.
examples.translation: The girl got distracted and lost sight of her parents.

examples.native: Dann sprach der Geist erneut, und seine Stimme klang wie das Seufzen des Windes.
examples.translation: Then the ghost spoke again, and his voice sounded like the sighing of the wind.

rules.title: Prepositions with case
rules.explanation: Mit, bei, nach, seit, von, zu and aus normally govern dative. Für, ohne and durch normally govern accusative. A preposition selects the case of its complement, not the case of every noun nearby.

examples.native: Tom wusste von nichts.
examples.translation: Tom knew nothing.

examples.native: Ich verspreche, von nun an nett zu euch zu sein.
examples.translation: I promise I'll be nice to you from now on.

examples.native: Ich wurde zu Unrecht angeklagt.
examples.translation: I was falsely accused.

rules.title: Two-way prepositions
rules.explanation: Many spatial uses take dative for location and accusative for a destination or change of spatial relation. The distinction is not simply movement versus no movement. A movement within a location can still take dative.

examples.native: Schauen Sie sich diese Fische im Teich an.
examples.translation: Look at those fish in the pond.

examples.native: Tom sollte in Kürze hier sein.
examples.translation: Tom should be here shortly.

examples.native: Die Jungen unterhielten sich über Videospiele.
examples.translation: The boys talked about video games.

rules.title: Past forms of sein and haben
rules.explanation: War and hatte are past forms of sein and haben. They occur frequently in spoken as well as written German. They also help construct pluperfect forms when a past participle follows.

examples.native: Wie waren eure letzten Prüfungen?
examples.translation: How were your last exams?

examples.native: Das war äußerst lustig.
examples.translation: It was extremely funny.

examples.native: Das war ein schwerwiegender Fehler.
examples.translation: That was a serious mistake.

rules.title: Participles in context
rules.explanation: A past participle can occur in a perfect, passive or adjective phrase. The auxiliary and context determine the construction. Gehen often forms its perfect with sein; many transitive verbs use haben.

examples.native: Weißt du, wie beschäftigt ich gewesen bin?
examples.translation: Do you know how busy I've been?

examples.native: Wer hat es ihm gesagt? Nicht vielleicht du?
examples.translation: Who told him? Not you, perhaps?

examples.native: Tom ist schon lange nicht mehr hier gewesen.
examples.translation: Tom hasn't been here in a long time.

rules.title: Werden: future and passive
rules.explanation: Werden plus infinitive can mark future or prediction; werden plus past participle can mark an event passive. The form alone is not enough: inspect the later verb and the whole meaning.

examples.native: Langsam werde ich neidisch.
examples.translation: I'm beginning to get jealous.

examples.native: Tom wird Vater sein.
examples.translation: Tom is going to be a father.

examples.native: Ich werde im Krankenhaus behandelt.
examples.translation: I am receiving treatment at the hospital.

rules.title: Conditional and polite forms
rules.explanation: Konjunktiv II marks hypothetical meaning and polite distance. Würde often combines with an infinitive; wäre and hätte are common direct forms. A hypothetical past uses hätte/wäre plus participle.

examples.native: Sie sagte, sie würde im nächsten Monat sechzehn.
examples.translation: She said she would be sixteen next month.

examples.native: Könnten Sie das noch einmal erklären?
examples.translation: Would you explain it again?

examples.native: Ich würde das gelbe nehmen.
examples.translation: I'll take the yellow one.

rules.title: Relative words
rules.explanation: A relative pronoun relates a clause to an antecedent. Its gender and number follow the antecedent, but its case follows its role inside the relative clause. The relative clause normally has verb-final order.

examples.native: Es lebe die Republik!
examples.translation: Long live the Republic!

examples.native: Du solltest die Menschen respektvoller behandeln.
examples.translation: You should treat people with more respect.

examples.native: Dem Mann droht die Todesstrafe.
examples.translation: The man is liable to the death penalty.

rules.title: Infinitives with zu
rules.explanation: Many infinitive complements use zu. Um ... zu expresses purpose when the understood subject fits. Zu can also be a preposition, so check whether a verb infinitive is present before analysing it as an infinitive marker.

examples.native: John ist zu dick, um schnell zu rennen.
examples.translation: John is too fat to run fast.

examples.native: Wir haben unser Leben zu leben.
examples.translation: We have our lives to live.

examples.native: Es bringt nichts, mit ihm zu streiten.
examples.translation: It is vain to argue with him.

rules.title: Comparison and quantity
rules.explanation: Comparatives normally use als, while equal comparison uses so ... wie. Mehr and weniger do not take the ordinary attributive adjective endings. Viel/viele distinguish some uncountable and countable uses.

examples.native: Wie viele Instrumente kannst du spielen?
examples.translation: How many instruments do you know how to play?

examples.native: Tom hat nicht sehr viel geholfen.
examples.translation: Tom didn't help much.

examples.native: Wie viel ist das insgesamt?
examples.translation: What is the total amount?

rules.title: Concession and argument
rules.explanation: Obwohl introduces a subordinate concession. Trotzdem, deshalb and jedoch can link main clauses as adverbials, so they interact with verb-second order. Distinguish concession from consequence in the translation.

examples.native: Du bist ein Hornochse, aber ich liebe dich trotzdem.
examples.translation: You're an idiot, but I still love you.

examples.native: Ich besitze keinen CD-Spieler, aber ich habe die CD trotzdem gekauft.
examples.translation: I don't have a CD player, but I bought the CD anyway.

examples.native: Obwohl sie alle anderen feige nennt, fehlt ihr selbst dennoch jeglicher Mut.
examples.translation: Although she calls all the others cowardly, she nonetheless lacks any courage herself.

Wenn ich einen Fehler mache, überprüfe ich die Regel und versuche es noch einmal. Mein Ziel ist es, Menschen zu verstehen und meine Gedanken klar auszudrücken.
passages.translation: I am learning a new language. Each day, I read a short text and listen to clear examples. I write useful words in a notebook. When I make a mistake, I check the rule and try again. My goal is to understand people and express my ideas clearly.

passages.title: Economics: opportunity cost
passages.native: Wer sich für eine Möglichkeit entscheidet, verzichtet zugleich auf andere Möglichkeiten. Die Kosten einer Entscheidung bestehen daher nicht nur aus dem Geld, das ausgegeben wird. Auch Zeit, Aufmerksamkeit und entgangene Chancen können relevant sein. Ein günstiger Kurs ist beispielsweise nicht unbedingt die beste Wahl, wenn er kaum zu den eigenen Zielen passt. Um Alternativen sinnvoll zu vergleichen, muss man zunächst klären, welche Ergebnisse wichtig sind. Dabei bleiben manche Werte schwer messbar. Eine sorgfältige Entscheidung kann diese Unsicherheit berücksichtigen, ohne so zu tun, als ließe sich jedes Ziel in einer einzigen Zahl ausdrücken.
passages.guide: Choosing one possibility also means forgoing others. A decision's costs therefore consist not only of money spent, but also time, attention and forgone opportunities. A cheap course may not be the best choice if it poorly fits one's goals. Comparing alternatives requires clarifying the desired outcomes. Some values are hard to measure; careful decisions can acknowledge uncertainty without pretending every goal fits one number.

grammarTerms: Noun
A word naming a person, thing or idea: student, book, freedom.
Verb
A word describing an action or state: read, know, be.
Subject
The participant linked to the main verb’s subject pattern. In The student reads a book, the student is the subject.
Object
A participant selected by a verb. In The student reads a book, a book is the direct object.
Agreement
One word changes to match another, for example an adjective matching a noun’s gender and number.
Case
A noun/pronoun form marking its relationship in a sentence. Cases can mark subjects, objects, possession or relations usually expressed by English prepositions.
Gender
A grammatical noun class. It does not always describe the sex of a person or any physical property.
Tense
A verb system that relates a situation to a time, often past or non-past.
Aspect
How a situation is viewed: unfolding, completed, habitual, experienced or in a resulting state.
Infinitive
A non-finite verb form often used for a dictionary entry or a complement. It does not by itself give the ordinary person/tense pattern.
Participle
A verb-derived form used in compound predicates or as a modifier; its exact function depends on the language and construction.
Clause
A unit organised around a predicate. One sentence can contain several clauses.
Register
Language choices suited to a situation: casual conversation, polite requests, academic writing or another context.
